My dog Kâsh, a boxer, developed sudden swelling and watery discharge in both eyes last night. I couldn't tell whether it was a bite or an allergic reaction, so I rushed him in as an emergency.

I called ahead around 9 p.m. to ask about wait times. The clerk on the phone would only say there were five patients ahead of us, with no estimate of how long that might take.

We checked in at 9:08 p.m. and were placed fifth in the queue. Fair enough, we were told there was a wait. But then we waited. It took more than three hours, until around 12:15 a.m., for my dog to finally reach the front of the line.

At 12:46 a.m., still not called back, I asked the front desk what to expect once we were in a room. A staff member came out, said something to the clerk I couldn't hear, and I was then told there would be another two-hour wait, on top of the three-plus hours we had already spent, before my dog would even be seen.

This clinic has no back entrance or triage bypass. Every animal that arrived during our wait, six or seven more after us, went through the same front-door check-in and queue I did. I did not see any patient treated with urgency ahead of the line, regardless of how their condition looked.

Nobody could explain why the clinic was averaging less than one patient seen per hour for what I was told were routine, non-critical cases: not surgeries, not major trauma. At that point, nearly four hours after arriving with a genuine emergency, I left without my dog being seen.

I want to be fair: the staff I spoke with were not rude to me personally. But a system where a pet can sit as the literal first in line and still face a two-hour wait, with six or seven sick animals stacking up behind, points to a real staffing or capacity problem. If your pet has anything less than a life-threatening emergency, I'd think hard before coming here at night.

Please think twice about bringing your fur babies here. I came in on Saturday midday because my Leo was having some breathing problems and low appetite. Dr. Pamintuan recommended bloodwork, fluids along with x-rays. Because he thought maybe there was a hairball in his stomach. I refuse x-rays because I knew he was showing symptoms of what could be a cold and I was thinking we would get prescribed antibiotics. The bloodwork was done as recommended. Platelets came back very low and Doctor said it was a Fluke. His RBC were also critically low. It also showed he was dehydrated. He then proceeded with his assessment and stated  Leo’s lungs were clear. He diagnosed him with anemia and dehydration. IV fluids were administered along with vitamin B 12. After the appointment, he was sent home with Bravecto Topical flea treatment, Anti-nausea medication and appetite stimulant. We went home and gave it to him as prescribed at around 7:20 PM. I woke up at 6 AM the next day and notice he was extremely lethargic. He was disoriented and started showing signs of mouth breathing. I called around eight to nine a.m. to let them know that he wasn’t doing good. Staff in the front said I refuse x-rays, so basically put me at fault. I had blood work done. Why was I sent home Without any antibiotic’s or any treatment for his anemia?   He still gave me Bravecto To treat his fleas And totally ignore the fact that he was having some congestion issues as I had stated. Anyhow, At around 4 PM I rushed him back to get seen because I could visually see he was not doing good.  They admitted him as triage. They put him in an oxygen chamber And gave him some more IV fluids. Blood work was then done along with x-rays. It was then confirmed he had severe pneumonia and fluids in his lungs. How did the doctor miss this? My poor Leo came in with  very little respiratory problems the day before as you see in the photo. How did His condition change  drastically in less than 24 hours of him seeing the provider. I’m sure he had an allergic reaction to flea medication. I don’t understand why it was prescribed knowing he already was anemic. My boy was  Hospitalize on critical care for about three nights. Blood work showed signs of improvement every single night so this gave us hope. They recommended we take him to see a cardiologist, but it was quoted at about 5-6K to be transferred with an ambulance. This is not including the overnight stay of $5000 at the specialty hospital to see a cardiologist. I felt trapped.  If my boy would have been given a different treatment the night before he got admitted, I’m 100% sure he would’ve made it. My boy died In the hands of mission veterinarian clinic . I tried everything to save him, but this careless doctor that saw him the night before only cared about  selling me useless products. He was only seven years old. He had so much life left. Not once did he get sick. Now I have to deal with grief and anger of failing him by going back to the place that misdiagnosed him. This grief will be in my heart for the rest of my life.

I wish I read these reviews before I brought my 9 year old English bulldog to this hospital. Shortly after I was asked to one of the rooms where one of the employees and told me that the estimate was a minimum of $2000 for some x-rays and oxygen and a blood test? I made the decision to move forward and paid the $2,000.00 (they called it deposit) as I felt I was doing the right thing for Molly and they would be providing help ease her respiratory distress. In hindsight my decision was purely emotional and they recognized that and presented their estimate as ncessary. I felt like I did not have a choice or not much of a choice.
They already had Molly in the back and I went out to the lobby. After about an hour I was called back into the office and was informed that they had completed the tests and that she would need to go to a specialist. I asked what is a specialist going to do and was told thst she might need some type of surgery to help with her breathing. Mind you these issue was brought on suddenly and I didn't understand what had changed to make her breathe in such a manner.
I told the doctor to give me referrals and I will decide on how I would like to proceed and told him that I would to take Molly home. He said "I don't advise it" and "that I would I would have to sign a waiver". I said that's fine I'll sign a waiver. A few minutes later they brought Molly out, she was wrapped in a dirty towel (which the guy told me I could keep) with her tongue hanging out of her mouth. I layed her down in the back seat of my car and tried to move her and she wouldn't move. She took one final shallow breath and she passed in my car. I am still in shock as to what happened. Save yourself a lot of grief and do some research before your bring your pet here.

On Sunday, we brought Coco in because she was not eating. We were told she physically appeared fine aside from pale gums. At no point were we clearly told her condition was urgent or life-threatening.
We were presented with approximately $1,200 in diagnostic testing — no treatment included, just tests. It was overwhelming. We were told we could at least proceed with bloodwork (close to $500) because it would “show us a lot” and give a big picture of what was going on internally since she physically appeared fine. Based on that reassurance, we agreed.
I directly asked the veterinary technician if there was any possibility she could die the next day. He laughed and said, “It’s not like that.” That statement reassured us she was not in immediate danger.
While Coco was in the back treatment area, I could hear her crying from the room we were placed in. When she was returned, she had a large visible fluid bump on her back from injections. It was never clearly explained how much fluid was administered or how it would affect her physically, especially considering she had not been eating.
The bloodwork reportedly showed a very high white blood cell count and a thyroid infection. Even with those findings, we were not told she was critical or at risk of sudden death. Instead, we were given two financial options: a $5,000 hospitalization plan or a lower-cost option around $450.
We could not afford the $5,000 hospitalization and declined it. I understand that this is considered declining recommended medical advice. However, what is deeply upsetting is that at no point were we clearly told that taking her home could mean she might not survive the day. No one said, “She could decline rapidly.” No one said, “She may not make it through today without hospitalization.”
We were told to return in one month to recheck bloodwork for $500— which strongly suggested she was stable enough to monitor.
Coco was discharged at 1:05 PM. Within an hour at home, she could barely walk. By 2:15 PM, she was vomiting and crying in agony. I called the clinic and was told this was “not normal,” but to continue monitoring her. I was not told to bring her back immediately.
By approximately 4:50–5:00 PM, Coco passed away — just hours after receiving care.
Afterward, the practice manager, Danny, and the chief medical officer, William, emphasized in EMAILS that I declined medical advice and referenced signed AMA documentation. I do not dispute that hospitalization was declined. What I question is the communication surrounding that decision.
It was only after Coco passed away that I LEARNED additional information that had NEVER been clearly explained to me. When I returned in person seeking answers and later reviewed the records, I saw in the notes written by Dr. Emmanuel Pimentel that there was concern documented about possible internal bleeding and that her prognosis was described as grave.
This was devastating to read.
If there was concern that she could be bleeding internally or might not survive, that SHOULD HAVE been communicated to ME clearly and directly before I made decisions. Instead, when I specifically asked if she could die the next day, I was told, “It’s not like that.”
Their follow-up emails focus heavily on paperwork, documentation, and declined services. They do not answer the core questions I ask:
Why was I reassured when I asked about the risk of death?
Why were the risks of taking her home not clearly explained in plain language?
Why was I not told to bring her back immediately when she began vomiting and crying in severe distress?
My dog died three hours after leaving this clinic.
Families deserve transparency, clarity, and compassion when their pet’s life may be at risk. We made decisions based entirely on what was verbally communicated to us at the time. If we had been clearly told that she could die within hours, we would have understood the gravity of the situation very differently and made different decisions such as hospitalization or just letting her pass naturally, not filled with injections and pills dying in agony pain.
